issue.title: Blackboard MVP (M0+M1): core-logic kernel, a Bb editor sort, and documentation slides
issue.body:
## Blackboard MVP: a proof assistant's core logic inside Hazel

An experiment: an MVP of **Blackboard**, a proposed "clean slate" proof assistant whose core logic has a type of all types, an internal typing relation, and no lambda. Two milestones are here.

**Try it:** Documentation → Blackboard → 0. Overview, at https://hazel.org/build/blackboard-mvp/

### M0 — the kernel

`src/language/blackboard/` — `BbTerm` (terms `x`, `t : T`, `type`, `(x : T₁) → T₂`, `t₁ t₂`; signatures, blocks, documents; substitution, α-equivalence, printing), `BbCheck` (the decidable fragment the paper calls `tychk`, without conversion), `BbError` (errors as data, located by signature entry), `BbParse` (the paper's concrete syntax, for fixtures). No dependency on tiles or the web layer.

Tests use the paper's own signatures as fixtures. The checker finds the paper's two slips in `cong-ap` (a name bound twice; a family used as a type) and the two in `int-elim` (missing arguments), and records where the paper's examples lean on equations the fragment cannot use.

### M1 — the editor sort

`Bb(BbSort.Term)` is a nested sort, following the ALFA derivation sub-language in `src/language/derivation/`: forms in `Form.re`, molding, `MakeTerm`, a pretty printer, and `blackboard ... end` to embed a document in an expression. `BbGrammar` / `BbTermBase` / `Bb` carry editor terms and read them back as kernel terms, entries, blocks and documents. Statics and the cursor inspector are M2, so an embedded document is inert for now.

Two decisions worth review:

- **The colon binds tighter than the arrow**, so `(x : A) -> x : B` reads as the paper writes it. In a signature entry the colon is a declaration instead, and is loosest; `Bb.rotate_entry` rotates the spine back, so `f : A -> B` declares `f` of type `A -> B`.
- **`Insert.effective_sort` no longer falls back to the enclosing sort inside Blackboard.** It is a closed sub-language, so a token with no Blackboard expansion stays a monotile. Without this, typing `type` inside a block expands into Hazel's `type _ = _ in`. This is the one change outside Blackboard-specific code that affects existing behaviour; it is guarded by `Sort.is_bb`.

### Documentation slides

Five slides under **Documentation → Blackboard**: Overview, Terms, Signatures, Checking, Metatheory. They load through the typing parser, since menhir has no Blackboard productions (as with the derivation sub-language). Both corpus ratchets ledger them with a reason, and `DocSlides.ReparseBackuptext` pins their text fidelity.

The `Bb` sort also needed a colour: with no entry in the token palette, Blackboard code rendered in the fallback colour and was effectively unreadable. Measured against the code background, it is now 6.49:1, where `Exp` is 5.33, `Typ` 4.19, `Drv` 3.73 and `Pat` 3.32.

`Test_BlackboardSlides` requires every shipped slide to read back as a document. It earns its place: three separate content bugs made part of a slide silently become a hole while the text still round-tripped. Hazel names cannot contain a hyphen, so `falsity-eq` was three tokens; `false` is a boolean literal, not a name; and `witness : a : A` associates as `(witness : a) : A`. Slides therefore use underscores where the paper uses hyphens, noted on the Terms slide. Behind two of them was a reader bug: a signature of three or more entries nests to the right, and only the top level was being read.

### `mech/`

The Rocq mechanization of the core logic (`Blackboard.v`, Rocq 9.2, no axioms) and its compile log, as the reference semantics: consistency of the bare logic, conservativity of construction blocks, and a five-point model. It covers both the rules as first printed and the author's corrected `arrow+`. Not part of the build.

### Testing

```
dune build test/idb_stub.js test/haz3ltest.bc.js --profile dev
bash test/run_node.sh test Blackboard
```

23 Blackboard tests pass. The full suite was run: the only failure was `Evaluator and stepper are consistent`, which is the known QCheck flake — it passed on three consecutive re-runs.

### Not in this PR

Implicit arguments, user-defined syntax, tactics, equational rewriting, Blackboard statics in the editor, and menhir support.

issue.title: Ascription steps make evaluation quadratic in call-stack depth (regression in Probes IV)
issue.body:
## Summary

An ascription evaluated inside a recursive call now does work proportional to the current call-stack depth. A linear program becomes quadratic, and past roughly 10k frames it dies with a JS heap OOM rather than merely running slowly. This regressed in Probes IV (#2363) — dev immediately before that merge is linear.

## Repro

```hazel
let sum : Int -> Int =
  fun n -> if n == 0 then 0 else n + (sum(n - 1) : ?) in
sum(12800)
```

`./hazel run`, wall clock, baseline startup ~1.1s:

| n | `ac4df9feef` (before Probes IV) | `a816823aee` (Probes IV) |
|---|---|---|
| 3200 | 1.20 | 1.50 |
| 6400 | 1.29 | 2.62 |
| 12800 | 1.49 | **OOM** |
| 25600 | 2.04 | **OOM** |

OOM is `FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit — JavaScript heap out of memory`. Every pre-merge run completes with the correct answer.

Delete the `: ?` and dev is linear again — 1.21 / 1.29 / 1.47 at 3200 / 6400 / 12800 — so it's the ascription, not the recursion.

## Cause

`Evaluator.re:246`, in the delegation bookkeeping Probes IV introduced:

```reason
(DHExp.rep_id(exp), CallStack.ids_of_stack(call_stack)),
```

`ids_of_stack` is `List.map((f: frame) => f.id, cs)` (`CallStack.re:29`) — O(stack depth), allocating a fresh list. It runs on every step whose kind is `may_delegate: true`, and per `Transition.re:186–188` those are exactly `Ascription`, `AscriptionTypAp` and `AscriptionAp`. One ascription step per frame at depth N gives Θ(N²) work, and since the entries are retained in `delegations`, Θ(N²) live memory — which is what actually kills it.

Counting the steps and summing the stack depth at each confirms the shape: 2000 steps → 1,997,003; 4000 → 7,994,003; 6000 → 17,991,003, i.e. k²/2.

Patching out only that `ids_of_stack` call restores linearity exactly: 1.23 / 1.32 / 1.52 / 2.02 at 3200 → 25600.

## Possible fixes

1. **Gate the insert on the redex id being a probe target.** The list is only consulted inside the `Some` branch of `switch (is_target)` at `Evaluator.re:298–302`, so an entry whose id isn't a target can never match. Semantics-preserving, and makes every unprobed program free. It does not fix a probed ascription inside deep recursion.
2. **Replace the materialized id list with a cheaper stack identity** — an incrementally maintained fingerprint, or keying on the stack value itself. This fixes it in general.

## Notes

Measured via the CLI on two worktrees at the commits above; the evaluator is untouched by any branch involved. `delegations` / `ids_of_stack` do not exist pre-merge (0 occurrences in `Evaluator.re` vs 26 after).

A linear program becomes quadratic, and past roughly 10k frames it dies with a JS heap OOM rather than merely running slowly. This regressed in Probes IV (#2363) — dev immediately before that merge is linear.

## Repro

```hazel
let sum : Int -> Int =
  fun n -> if n == 0 then 0 else n + (sum(n - 1) : ?) in
sum(12800)
```

`./hazel run`, wall clock, baseline startup ~1.1s:

| n | `ac4df9feef` (before Probes IV) | `a816823aee` (Probes IV) |
|---|---|---|
| 3200 | 1.20 | 1.50 |
| 6400 | 1.29 | 2.62 |
| 12800 | 1.49 | **OOM** |
| 25600 | 2.04 | **OOM** |

OOM is `FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit — JavaScript heap out of memory`. Every pre-merge run completes with the correct answer.

Delete the `: ?` and dev is linear again — 1.21 / 1.29 / 1.47 at 3200 / 6400 / 12800 — so it's the ascription, not the recursion.

## Cause

`Evaluator.re:246`, in the delegation bookkeeping Probes IV introduced:

```reason
(DHExp.rep_id(exp), CallStack.ids_of_stack(call_stack)),
```

`ids_of_stack` is `List.map((f: frame) => f.id, cs)` (`CallStack.re:29`) — O(stack depth), allocating a fresh list. It runs on every step whose kind is `may_delegate: true`, and per `Transition.re:186–188` those are exactly `Ascription`, `AscriptionTypAp` and `AscriptionAp`. One ascription step per frame at depth N gives Θ(N²) work, and since the entries are retained in `delegations`, Θ(N²) live memory — which is what actually kills it.

Counting the steps and summing the stack depth at each confirms the shape: 2000 steps → 1,997,003; 4000 → 7,994,003; 6000 → 17,991,003, i.e. k²/2.

Patching out only that `ids_of_stack` call restores linearity exactly: 1.23 / 1.32 / 1.52 / 2.02 at 3200 → 25600.

## Possible fixes

1. **Gate the insert on the redex id being a probe target.** The list is only consulted inside the `Some` branch of `switch (is_target)` at `Evaluator.re:298–302`, so an entry whose id isn't a target can never match. Semantics-preserving, and makes every unprobed program free. It does not fix a probed ascription inside deep recursion.
2. **Replace the materialized id list with a cheaper stack identity** — an incrementally maintained fingerprint, or keying on the stack value itself. This fixes it in general.

## Notes

Measured via the CLI on two worktrees at the commits above; the evaluator is untouched by any branch involved. `delegations` / `ids_of_stack` do not exist pre-merge (0 occurrences in `Evaluator.re` vs 26 after).

review.body: Three bugs from a review pass, each with a reproduction. Inline below.

comment.body:
**`type_of_sample` runs statics on an already-elaborated value using the source context's `use_mode`, so the sample gets re-kinded a second time.**

`ctx` here comes from `Info.ctx_of(info.statics)`, i.e. the ambient source mode. `Ctx.re:45` documents the field as `use_mode: option(Operators.mode) // None if elaboration has already occurred`, and `CachedStatics.re:101` passes `Builtins.ctx_init(is_dynamic_term ? None : Some(Int))` for exactly this reason. With `use_mode = Some(Nat)`, `Operators.replace_literal`'s `(Int(n), _, Some(Nat)) => Nat(n)` arm retypes an `Int` sample as `Nat`.

Repro:

```
let f : Int -> Int = fun x -> x + 1 in
use Nat in
^^statics(f(3))
```

`f` is `Int -> Int` and the value is `4`, so both static modes show `Int` — but Dynamic mode shows **`Nat`**, in green as runtime-derived. (Confirmed in the browser.)

Fix: `Ctx.set_use_mode(ctx, None)` before `Statics.mk`. `TypeProj.re:34`'s `Builtins.ctx_init(Some(Int))` fallback has the same problem.

**This is the only `Sample.mk` site that substitutes the environment into the sample value.**

The other three (`RecordPrint` just below, `RecordPatMatch`, `ObsTrace.SpanClose`) pass the value as-is and let `Sample.Env.elide` substitute lazily, per captured binding. Substituting here also breaks `Substitution.re`'s documented PRECONDITION ("the environment should list all free variables (each free variable in the env should just be v |-> v)") — a raw mid-evaluation env is not of that shape — and costs a deep `Exp.replace_all_ids` copy plus a recursive re-substitution for every bound variable it hits, over an env that includes all of `Builtins.env_init`, per ascription sample, inside evaluation.

Two visible consequences, both against a control probe on the same value:

```
let n = 41 in
^^probe((fun y -> y + n) : ?)   ->  fun y -> y + 41     # this path: env inlined
^^probe(fun y -> y + n)         ->  fun y -> y + n      # every other probe
^^probe((fun n -> n + 1) : ?)   ->  fun n' -> n' + 1    # binder alpha-renamed
```

The last one is the one a user would report: the probe shows a function whose parameter has been renamed, purely because the term sits under a nested ascription.

Fix: drop the substitution and let Sample's env elision do it.

**Ascription samples are collected before `req_final`, so a probe can report unevaluated syntax as a runtime value.**

This first `Ascriptions.transition` runs on the raw `d`; only the `None` branch goes on to `req_final`. When it returns `Some`, the samples it emitted hold the pre-evaluation operand (env-substituted, but not reduced), so `DynamicTypInfer.type_of_sample` ends up running statics over *syntax* and the "dynamic" type collapses to the static result type for that sample.

Repro:

```
let f = fun x -> x + 1 in
if true then ^^probe(f(3) : ?) else 2
```

```
$ ./hazel probe --many b.hz
if true then ⟦f(3) : ?⟧ else 2     ≡ ^^fold((fun x -> x + 1))(3)
```

Drop the `: ?` and the same probe reads `≡ 4`. Only one sample is recorded, so the bogus one is what the UI shows. A `case` rule triggers it identically; a `let` def does not, because it gets no outer ascription — the trigger is an ascription nested inside something `fresh_ascription` wraps (`if` branches, `case` rules, list elements).

Fix: collect only on the post-`req_final` path.

issue.title: Projector `dynamics` flag has had no reader since the MakeTerm probe rework
issue.body:
`Projector.dynamics: bool` (`ProjectorBase.re:209`, forwarded by `Cook` at `:271`) is documented as "this projector will be instrumented with a probe to collect dynamic information during evaluation", but nothing reads it.

It was added in 99b100f72f (2024-12-29, "projector API flag for dynamics collection") with a real consumer: `MakeTerm.should_instrument` looked it up to decide whether a probe-wrapped term actually received a `Probe` wrapper at parse time —

```reason
| (label, [Exp(body)]) when is_probe_wrap(label) =>
  ret(should_instrument(Exp.rep_id(body)) ? Parens(body, Probe(...)) : body.term)
```

That consumer was removed in 9a8cd47887 (2026-01-08, "rm legacy probe code in maketerm") and nothing replaced it. `ProjectorInfo.mk_info` now populates `info.dynamics` from the dynamics map regardless of the flag, so a projector's declared value has no effect either way.

Consequences: the declaration is misleading — someone tracing where a projector's samples come from is sent to a dead end, and setting it `true` on a new projector looks like opting in when it does nothing. Ten implementations plus the signature carry a value nobody consumes.

Either give it a consumer (if per-projector gating of sample collection is still wanted) or delete it from the signature, `Cook`, and the ten implementations. Removal touches 11 files for zero behaviour change, which is why it wants its own PR rather than riding along with feature work.

issue.title: Rich table probe: the column (⋮) menu opens at the bottom of the drawer instead of under the column header
issue.body:
Since #2363 — specifically `7428e0e88b`, which retired the anchored modal.

### Repro

Open a table rich probe in the drawer with few enough rows that the drawer doesn't scroll, then click a column's ⋮. The menu appears below the bottom edge of the table rather than under that column's header.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0dbcc198-08bf-4da4-bcd6-6a41198c4d60

### Why

- The `.cm-*` rules place the menu with `top: 100%; left: 0` and are documented as anchoring "inside the `<th>` cell" (`proj-table-probe.css:34-68`). Those offsets resolve against the nearest **positioned** ancestor.
- The only rule that ever made the `th` positioned is `.modal .table th { position: relative }` (`proj-table-probe.css:138-146`), and `.modal` is no longer rendered: `let modal_nodes = []; let _unused_modal = modal_overlay;` (`ProbeProj.re:2489-2492`).
- So the containing block is now `.below-wrapper .rich-drawer { position: relative }` (`proj-probe.css:822-824`) — and `top: 100%` is the bottom of the whole drawer.
- Corroboration: a **tall** table gets `.below-wrapper .rich-drawer.overflowing .table th { position: sticky }` (`proj-probe.css:844-847`), which does establish a containing block, so those tables place correctly. Only short / non-overflowing drawer tables are wrong.
- `Menu.direction_from_id` (`src/util/Menu.re:538-546`) measures the ⋮ button against `#main` and only picks a class name; placement is entirely CSS. The flip decision is honest; the anchor is wrong.

### Suggested fix

Give the header cell a containing block that doesn't depend on the retired modal — e.g. `.table th:has(> .column-menu) { position: relative }`, or hang it off the `menu-open` class the `th` already gets while its menu is open (`TableRenderer.re:433-441`). An unconditional `.table th { position: relative }` would fight the two `position: sticky` rules (`proj-probe.css:844`, `proj-table.css:63`).

### Cleanup that belongs with the fix

Retiring the modal left dead code behind, and that is what broke this anchor:

- `modal_overlay` is unreachable, kept alive only by `let _unused_modal = modal_overlay;` (`ProbeProj.re:2370-2414`, `:2489-2492`).
- The whole `.modal …` block in `proj-table-probe.css:80-169` is orphaned.
- The `nut-menu` class in the column menu's class list is inert — every `nut-menu.css` rule is scoped to `#top-bar`.

issue.title: No probe (sample context) menu in drawer mode
issue.body:
Since #2363 introduced drawer mode.

The sample context menu — pin, step into, `View as …` / `Hide …`, call display, environment — opens on right/alt-click of a sample chip (`.value`, `ProbeProj.re:723-750`). In the drawer that chip is not reachable, so the menu can't be opened for anything shown there.

### With a rich renderer active

The drawer content **replaces the sample views wholesale**:

```reason
switch (empty_status, rich_content) {
| (None, Some(content)) => [content]     /* ProbeProj.re:2054-2057 */
| (None, None) => ... sample_view ...
```

so there is no `.sample` / `.value` node in the drawer at all — no `on_contextmenu` (the repo has exactly two: `ProbeProj.re:718` and `CodeEditable.re:1087`) and no `sample-context-menu` node. A right-click over the table bubbles out — the projector wrapper deliberately passes right-clicks through (`ProjectorView.re:283-292`) — and opens the **editor** context menu, which has no `Hide table`.

### With plain samples in the drawer

Reported broken too. Here the chips *are* rendered (`~display=Block`) and the menu is meant to be promoted to a `FloatingElement` so `.below-wrapper`'s overflow can't clip it (`ProbeProj.re:1294-1309`, `proj-probe.css:1006-1011`) — so that promotion path needs checking as well.

### Why it matters

The context menu is the only place offering `Hide table` / `View as table`, so once a rich view is in the drawer the menu that would turn it off is unreachable from it. The only exits are the drawer's `×` — which exists only when `active_renderer != None`, so auto-rich drawers have none (`ProbeProj.re:2484`) — the nav-bar chevron, and ⌘↑/Escape, and none of those clear `active_renderer` (see #2519).

### Suggested direction

Give the drawer its own right-click surface that opens the indicated sample's context menu (the drawer already takes keyboard focus and knows the indicated sample, `ProbeProj.re:2040-2052`) instead of falling through to the editor menu.

issue.title: Rich probe: exiting drawer mode leaves the renderer active with nothing rendered ("Hide table" on a table that isn't shown)
issue.body:
Regression since #2363.

### Repro

1. Probe an expression whose value is a list of tuples with 4+ rows.
2. Right-click the sample → **View as table**. The table needs more than `inline_rows_cap = 4` rows, so it can't embed in the sample chip; activation implicitly opens the drawer and the table renders between the lines.
3. Click the nav-bar chevron (`Toggle drawer (⌘↓ / ⌘↑)`), or press ⌘↑ or Escape.
4. The sample reverts to abbreviated text — the table is gone from the screen.
5. Right-click the sample again: the menu still reads **`Hide table`**, not `View as table`.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d55f92a6-d5eb-432c-b975-52ba7f065538

### Why

- `ToggleDrawerMode` / `SetDrawerMode(false)` flip only `drawer_mode`; `active_renderer` stays `Some(table)` (`ProbeProj.re:2294-2309`).
- Offsides, a rich view embeds in the chip only when `drawer_rows <= inline_rows_cap` (`ProbeProj.re:772-787`, cap at `:361`), and for a table `drawer_rows = List.length(rows) + 1` (`TableRenderer.re:51`). The anchored modal that used to host it is retired (`let modal_nodes = [];`, `ProbeProj.re:2489-2492`). So there is nowhere left for it to render.
- The menu label is keyed on the model alone, not on whether anything is on screen:

```reason
let is_active = ctx.active_renderer_id == Some(r.id);
let label = (is_active ? "Hide " : "View as ") ++ r.id;   /* ProbeProj.re:1022-1025 */
```

### Effect

The label is wrong, and recovering the table takes two menu trips: `Hide table` (clears `active_renderer`) then `View as table` (recomputes `wants_drawer` and reopens the drawer).

### Suggested fix

Make the item a toggle over "is something actually rendered" rather than "is a renderer selected": either clear `active_renderer` when leaving the drawer if the renderer can't render inline, or derive `is_active` from the rendered surfaces and let a click on an already-selected renderer re-open the drawer.

### Adjacent, same predicate

`ToggleModal` ignores its payload whenever any renderer is already active (`ProbeProj.re:2351-2354`), so `View as card` while `table` is active just deactivates the table instead of switching renderers.

issue.title: Rich probe: exiting drawer mode leaves the renderer active with nothing rendered ("Hide table" on a table that isn't shown)
issue.body:

2. Right-click the sample → **View as table**. The table needs more than `inline_rows_cap = 4` rows, so it can't embed in the sample chip; activation implicitly opens the drawer and the table renders between the lines.
3. Click the nav-bar chevron (`Toggle drawer (⌘↓ / ⌘↑)`), or press ⌘↑ or Escape.

+  *survive* re-parsing inside a container (e.g. a fillable list element), prefer
+  the explicit hole token `?` — `[?]` round-trips, whereas implicit `[¿]` may

comment.body:
🤖 Recording an idea from discussion, **not** doing it here: the flag could go away entirely, with `append_exp` capturing the trailing value into `answer` while leaving the impl's own bindings in scope.

All 25 lessons already end in the expression that is the answer — the 20 plain ones as a let-chain ending in `first_four` / `triple(10)` / `table`, the 5 wrapper ones as a bare expression like `2 + ¿`. So the flag's only job is choosing which of two things the tests see: the impl's names *or* `answer`. Nothing requires that to be either/or:

```
<bindings> in let answer = <trailing expr> in <tests>
```

gives both. The wrapper lessons' tests keep using `answer`, the others keep using their own names, and no lesson binds `answer` itself so there is no shadowing. It is statics-neutral: today's join is `Seq(trailing_expr, tests)`, and `Seq` synthesizes its first operand with no expectation and adds no marks, as does an unannotated `let` pattern — and there is no unused-binding mark to trip on. It would also fix something small: `Seq` evaluates that trailing expression and discards the value, so today the last line of those 20 lessons is decorative as far as the tests are concerned. Implementation is a generalization of the walk `append_exp` already does through `Let`/`Seq`/`Filter`/`Theorem` bodies.

Two caveats for whoever picks it up: `answer` would mean "value of the trailing expression", which is not always the graded artifact (for the function lessons the last line is a demo call, so `answer` is `30`, not `triple`); and `wrapper: bool` is a field of `p('code)`, which derives sexp/yojson, so dropping it changes a serialized shape that student progress may be stored in.

**Why not now:** it changes `Tutorial.re`'s semantics and every lesson file, which would make integrating @disconcision's tutorials harder later. Not worth the divergence for a cleanup. Leaving the flag as-is and documented.

issue.title: Delete Util.Either: result where it means success-or-failure, Core.Either where it means a partition
issue.body:
Follows up [a review comment on #2439](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2439#discussion_r3830911397) asking whether `Either` isn't already built into OCaml. It is — twice — and ours was redundant, but the call sites turned out to want two different things.

## Why ours had to go

`src/util/Either.re` was four lines: `type t('l, 'r) = L('l) | R('r)` with `show`/`sexp`/`yojson`. Those derivations were dead — no `[@deriving]` type in the tree embeds an `Either.t`, which was the one plausible reason to keep our own over Core's.

It also **shadowed Core's**. Every library that uses it has `-open Core` in its dune, and every file that uses it also does `open Util`, which lands second, so `Core.Either` was unreachable without qualifying it.

## What the call sites actually wanted

Of 24 references, 20 were success-or-failure wearing the wrong constructors:

| Site | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `Operators.re` (13) | `Either.t(Atom.t, bad_literal)` | `result(Atom.t, bad_literal)` |
| `Atom.re` (3) | `Either.t('b, InvalidOperationError.t)` | `result('b, InvalidOperationError.t)` |
| `Transition.re` (4) | `Either.L(return_value)` / `Either.R(error)` | `Ok` / `Error` |
| `MatchedTyp.args` | `Either.t('a, int)` | `result(list(Typ.t), int)` |

`result` puts the error direction in the type instead of leaving it to a convention about which side `R` is, and `MatchedTyp.args` gets a concrete ok type rather than the `'a` it was carrying.

Only **`Aba.split`** and its single caller **`Segment.split_by_matching`** genuinely partition — each element goes to the A-stream or the B-stream, and neither side is an error. Those take `Core.Either`'s `First`/`Second`.

`src/util/Either.{re,rei}` and `Util`'s re-export of it are deleted. Removing the module made `open Util` dead in `MatchedTyp.re`, so that went too.

`BuiltinsADT`'s `Either` is the Hazel-language type alias — a different thing entirely — and is untouched.

## Verification

- `dune build @check --profile release` clean (no warnings)
- `make dev` clean
- `make test-quick`: 3556 tests pass

No behavior change is intended: this is a type-and-constructor rename, plus one type made less general.

issue.title: A lone ¿ inside a container is dropped by the text round-trip: [¿] reloads as []
issue.body:
`MarkerParse.of_text` recovers Grout by *deleting* the `¿` marker tile and letting the load-time regrout put Grout back — `strip_implicit_holes` does `Select.tile` then `Destruct.go` ([`src/haz3lcore/zipper/MarkerParse.re:94-111`](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/blob/dev/src/haz3lcore/zipper/MarkerParse.re#L94-L111)). That only recovers a hole where regrout would independently place one, so a marker whose removal leaves a **complete** term is lost.

The reachable case is a hole as a container's sole element:

| authored | after one round-trip | |
|---|---|---|
| `[¿]` | `[]` | ✗ dropped |
| `[¿, 1]` | `[¿, 1]` | ✓ |
| `[1, ¿]` | `[1, ¿]` | ✓ |
| `(¿, 1)` | `(¿, 1)` | ✓ |
| `let x = ¿ in x` | `let x = ¿ in x` | ✓ |

Delete the marker in `[¿]` and `[]` is already a well-formed empty list, so regrout has no reason to insert anything.

This is a persistence bug, not just a notational one: grout inside `[]` is a state the editor reaches by typing — inserting a space in `[|]` gives `[ <>|]`, per example III of #1077 — and `to_text` prints it as `[¿]`, so the document does not survive a reload. Same shape as #2450 (a dangling `;` dropping every probe pin from the round-trip), which was fixed.

## Repro

Put `let xs : [Int] = [¿] in xs` in a tutorial lesson's `@code` and run `./hazel tutorial-verify --verbose`:

```
List Literals                      impl:MISMATCH  tests:OK
  --- impl before roundtrip ---
let xs : [Int] = [¿] in
xs
  --- impl after roundtrip ---
let xs : [Int] = [] in
xs
```

## Fix direction

Replace the marker tile with a Grout piece directly instead of destruct-then-regrout, so an authored hole is preserved wherever it was written rather than only where regrout independently agrees one belongs.

## Related

Two changes to how CI reports, and how far it searches.

**Weekly Extended Tests.** New `.github/workflows/extended-tests.yml` runs Sundays against `dev` (plus `workflow_dispatch` with `factor`/`seed`), calling a new `make ci-extended`: the whole suite with `QCHECK_LONG=1`, so every QCheck `~count` is multiplied by `QCHECK_LONG_FACTOR`. Per-push CI runs each property once, so a property that fails on one seed in a few hundred never surfaces. The job pins its seed and writes the reproducing `QCHECK_*` command to its summary. It gates nothing — a red run is a bug report.

The default factor is 100 because `Slow` turns out not to mean `QCheck`: 237 tests carry the tag, only 12 are properties, so the factor scales a minority of the run and the rest is a fixed floor. That puts it at roughly 3.7 h on CI against GitHub's 6 h cap. Correct it from the first real run.

**Test reports move off the Deploy job.** `checks.yml` passed `use-actions-summary: false` to `dorny/test-reporter@v1`, but that input doesn't exist until v2 — it was ignored and a check run was always created. GitHub picks which of a commit's check suites a check run joins, and it picked Deploy's, so test results rendered under `Deploy branch preview` and a red suite made the deploy look broken. On `@v3` the default writes the report to the running job's summary and creates no check run, which is the only placement we control.

The table now appears on the `Fast checks` / `Full tests` summaries; the `Test Report` and `Quick Test Report` rows and their inline annotations go away. Nothing is lost as a gate — those jobs already fail on a red suite, and the report checks could never have been required, since fork PRs skip them. Consequently `checks: write` is gone, and `publish-reports` (which now only gated Codecov) is renamed `upload-coverage`, with fork PRs getting their reports too.

Comments in these files lost their measured numbers in favour of the reasoning and how to re-measure — the `~32-min suite` note was already wrong at 18, and the `~92%` beside it is what made factor 8 look like four hours.

**Verifying.** This PR's CI run should show the results table under Fast checks and Full tests, with no report rows under Deploy. `extended-tests.yml` can't run until it's on `dev`; after merge, `gh workflow run "Extended Tests" --ref dev -f factor=1` smoke-tests it in a couple of minutes.

issue.title: Modules II, part 9: the standard library as modules (proof of concept)
issue.body:
> [!WARNING]
> **Proof of concept, like #2508, and not close to done.** It exists to show
> what the standard library looks like once modules are real values, and to
> find out what that costs. Read "Known gaps" before reviewing anything else.

Ninth of the stack, on top of #2508. The standard library becomes modules,
and ships the vocabulary the implicits feature needs.

```
List.map([1, 2, 3], fun x -> x * 2)          -- [2, 4, 6]
String.of_int(42) ++ String.uppercase("ok")  -- "42OK"
Float.sqrt(9.0) >. Float.pi                  -- false
Option.map((Some(2), fun x -> x + 1))        -- Some(3)

let implicit A = ShowInt in
let show = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> S.show(x) in
show(3)                                      -- "3"
```

## What it does

- **Six modules**: `List` (all 65 list functions), `String`, `Int`, `Float`,
  `Option`, `Pair`. The list family is the one that crowds the namespace
  worst: `map`, `filter`, `length`, `find` and `head` are all top-level
  names today.
- **Every flat name stays.** `String.length` and `string_length` are the
  same function, so no program, slide or exercise changes meaning. The
  modules are the front door from here on; nothing is deprecated in this PR.
- **Both halves are derived from the same records.** A module builtin is an
  ordinary constant whose type is a signature and whose value is a module,
  and the signature's member types and the module's member values come from
  the same builtin, so a member cannot drift from the function it names. A
  member is the implementation, not a copy: it is the term the flat name is
  bound to.
- **`SHOW` and `ORD` ship as signature types**, with an instance per base
  type: `ShowInt`, `ShowFloat`, `ShowBool`, `ShowString`, `OrdInt`,
  `OrdFloat`, `OrdString`. Each carries a manifest type member, since
  resolution selects on it.

## Two decisions worth arguing with

**The instances are not ambient.** A program marks what it wants, one line
per instance. Making them ambient is a language decision rather than a
library one, and it needs a priority or coherence rule first: with none, a
program that defines its own instance for a base type under any other name
makes every call ambiguous against the shipped one. Twelve of the implicits
tests change meaning when they are ambient, which is the same warning from
the other side. The cost is a `let implicit A = ShowInt in` line, which is
what the Module Implicits slide already writes.

**No `EQ`.** Polymorphic `==` already compares two values of a type, so an
equality signature earns its keep only once a type can choose its own
equality, which wants the sharing constraint #2495 lacks.

## Two prerequisites this found, fixed where they belong

Both are in #2493, with tests, because plain source hits them:

- A module member's name is its label, but substitution renamed it away from
  capture like any binder, so `M.x` stopped finding it. The stepper
  substitutes the whole builtin environment, so any module with a member
  named after a builtin lost that member.
- A capitalized module name parses as a constructor, and a known constructor
  won, so a module whose name matched one could not be projected at all. The
  JSON type contributes `List`, `Int`, `String`, `Float` and `Bool` to every
  program's constructor namespace, which made exactly the five most useful
  stdlib names unusable: `module List = { let f = 1 } in List.f` was an
  error. Projecting a constructor means nothing, so the module now wins in
  dot position, and `List([Int(2)])` still builds JSON.

The one change here is in the evaluator: a member holding a fixpoint has to
unroll, so a projection judges a definition the way a variable lookup does,
sharing one predicate. Only a module that came out of the environment can
hit it, which is why it is in this PR rather than #2493.

## Known gaps

1. **Cost per mention.** A module out of the environment is copied on each
   mention, so `List.map` copies a 65-member module where `map` copies one
   fixpoint. I have not measured it against a hot loop, and if it matters the
   answer is probably to bind the library once per program rather than to
   hand it out of the environment, which needs a prelude mechanism that does
   not exist.
2. **The grouping is partial.** The tuple-label operations, the ADT helpers,
   the `Ord` inversion, `print`, the SInt and Nat families and the remaining
   conversions are still only flat. `Bool` has nothing worth grouping yet.
3. **`Int`, `Float` and `String` cannot be *declared* as modules in the text
   grammar**, since those are base-type tokens: `module Int = {…}` does not
   parse, though the shipped ones are fine because nothing declares them in
   source. The editor accepts it.
4. **Nothing is deprecated.** Two names for every function is the price of
   not breaking programs, and there is no mechanism to mark the flat ones
   legacy.
5. **No `List` for other collections.** There is no `Set`, `Map` or `Seq`
   because there are no such builtins; this PR groups what exists.
6. **`Option`'s type member is `Option`'s sum type**, so `Option.T` names it,
   but the module cannot expose the constructors: constructors declared in a
   module are not members of it (#2243).

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make ci-check` clean under the release profile ·
`make test-quick` 3845 green · new suites `Statics.BuiltinsModules` (11) and
`Evaluator.BuiltinsModules` (10), including that a member equals its flat
function and that a recursive member unrolls through a projection · CLI
probes for every module and for both signatures.

Expect the same two per-seed `Full tests` failures as the rest of the stack,
both unrelated and both dev's: the cyclic-alias crash in normalization and
the `:+` printer divergence explained on #2493.

issue.title: Modules II, part 8: modular implicits (proof of concept, not close to done)
issue.body:
> [!WARNING]
> **This is a proof of concept and is not close to done.** It is not intended to
> merge as it stands. Its purpose is to show that modular implicits fit Hazel's
> module system and to make one design concrete enough to argue about. The
> syntax, the resolution rule and the error reporting should all be expected to
> change. Please read "Known gaps" at the bottom before reviewing anything else,
> and treat everything above it as a sketch rather than a proposal.

Eighth of the stack, on top of #2503. A function parameter component can be
declared implicit, and a call that leaves it out has it filled in by the type
checker from the instances in scope.

```
type SHOW = { type T; let show : T -> String } in
let implicit ShowInt = { type T = Int; let show = string_of_int } in
let implicit ShowBool = { type T = Bool; let show = fun b -> if b then "true" else "false" } in
let show = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> S.show(x) in
   -- show : (implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String
show(3) ++ show(true)     -- "3true": S resolved to ShowInt, then ShowBool
show(ShowBool, true)      -- passed by hand: the arity includes S
```

## What it does

- `implicit S : SIG` is a pattern form (`Pat.Implicit`) and, in an arrow
  domain, a type form (`Typ.Implicit`). Functions stay uncurried: the binder is
  a component of the parameter, and it scopes over the later components and the
  codomain, so `(implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String` is an ordinary arrow type.
- `let implicit M = ...`, and the same as a module item, declare an instance
  (`Ctx.ImplicitEntry`). Only such bindings take part in resolution. A binder is
  itself an instance inside the function body, so implicit functions compose.
- At a call, arity decides: the explicit arity resolves every implicit, the full
  arity passes them by hand, and a mix is disambiguated by signature. Resolution
  keeps the instances whose type fits the signature, then narrows by the
  explicit arguments' types and the expected type. One left is the instance;
  none or several is a mark on the application, with a hole passed in the
  instance's place so evaluation proceeds around the error.
- The instance is spliced into the elaborated argument, so the runtime sees an
  ordinary application and the stepper shows `show(ShowInt, 3)`.
- A failed resolution names what the call required, not just the signature:
  `No implicit instance of SHOW with T = String for S`.

New module `src/language/statics/Implicits.re` holds the resolution; `docs/modules.md`
has a section on it, and the new "Module Implicits" doc slide is the worked example.

## Known gaps

Design questions left open, roughly in the order I would want them settled:

1. **Gradual typing weakens resolution.** An instance member written without an
   annotation types as `? -> String`, which fits every `{ let show : X -> String }`,
   so instances become interchangeable and calls turn ambiguous. The workaround
   in the docs (annotate members, use a manifest `type T = E.T`) is a workaround,
   not an answer. This is the part I trust least.
2. **A plain module parameter still loses the caller's type equation**, though
   it no longer loses it silently. #2498 now closes the parameter as well as
   the body, so the same program is an error rather than an unchecked call:

   ```
   let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
      mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature

   let dup = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- error: Expecting type String, String but got inconsistent type
      ShowInt.T, ShowInt.T
   ```

   An implicit binder is the only type in the language that can hold what the
   caller knows, which is why the second version checks and the first only
   reports its loss. Marking the parameter implicit is a workaround; the fix
   is a dependent domain for ordinary module parameters, the way Scala's
   dependent method types work, reusing the scoping and substitution this PR
   adds, or an ML sharing constraint. Three tests in
   `Test_Statics_Implicits` pin both halves.


3. **Error attribution.** Both resolution marks sit on the application. That was
   a deliberate choice and it still reads oddly in at least one case on the doc
   slide. Narrowing also runs only when more than one candidate fits the
   signature, so a single unfitting instance reports an argument mismatch
   (`expecting ShowInt.T, got String`) instead of a missing instance. The
   candidate list in an error is every instance in scope rather than the ones
   that fit the signature, and the ambiguity message never says that nothing in
   the call constrained the binder.
4. **No implicit functors.** Instances cannot themselves take implicit
   parameters, so there is no `SHOW` for `[T]` derived from `SHOW` for `T` and no
   recursive search. That is the main thing modular implicits are for, and it is
   entirely absent.
5. **Not supported anywhere else.** `DeferredAp` with implicit components;
   resolving an implicit function that is merely mentioned rather than applied;
   any spelling of `module implicit M : S = ...`.
6. **Cost.** The argument is type-checked twice at an implicit call (a probe pass
   decides the arity), so those applications pay double.
7. **Syntax warts.** `implicit` is now a keyword. A lone
   `implicit S : SIG -> τ` needs parentheses in both the editor and the text
   grammar. The keyword needs two different tile shapes, one per sort, for
   precedence reasons.
8. **Type equality is inconsistent about binder names.** `meet`/`ana_meet`
   rename binders positionally, while `Equality` and `equal_up_to_aliases`
   compare them literally, so `fast_equal` distinguishes types that are
   consistent.
9. **No instance coherence check.** Nothing notices that two instances
   overlap; you find out at a call site, as an ambiguity. A canonicity or
   orphan rule would move that error to the declaration, where it belongs.

Two pre-existing bugs are fixed on the way, both in commit 1: the editor read
`A -> M.T` as `(A -> M).T` because the type-level dot bound looser than the
arrow, and the pattern-annotation printer was not idempotent (`x:(S.T)`
reprinted as `x:((S.T))`).

## Verification

Editor behavior was checked by hand; anything that turned up is tracked
outside this PR.


`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` 3840 green · `Statics.Properties`,
`MenhirFuzz` (several seeds), `MenhirCorpus` and the reparse suites green ·
`hazel analyze`/`run` on a 14-function example program and on the new doc slide.
New suites: `Statics.Implicits` (39), `Evaluator.Implicits` (15),
`Typ.Implicit` (9), `Editing.Implicit` (4), plus Menhir, MakeTerm, ExpToSegment,
Elaboration, Equality, Abbreviate and ExplainThis cases.

## Stack note

Parts 3 to 7 were force-pushed with this: a Coverage crash on `case m.x` with an
abstract `m.T` is fixed where it was introduced (#2495, "a stuck path type is
opaque, not non-normalized") and cascaded up the stack. No other change to those
branches.

issue.title: Stack overflow crash on programs nested ~125 deep (e.g. 125 let-in lines)
issue.body:
Pasting this into an empty scratch editor on https://hazel.org/build/dev/ (Chrome) shows the crash page "Exception during Calculate: Stack overflow":

```
let a0 = 0 in
let a1 = 1 in
...
let a124 = 124 in
a0
```

Generate it with `python3 -c "print('\n'.join(f'let a{i} = {i} in' for i in range(125)) + '\na0')" | pbcopy`, then Cmd+V. 100 lines works; 125 crashes about a second after the paste. `1 + (1 + (1 + ...` nested 150 deep crashes the same way, while a flat program of the same size (a 1000-element list literal, ~2000 tokens) is fine, so the trigger is nesting depth, not program size. Typing or loading such a program hits it too, since every edit re-runs the same pass.

A CPU profile at the crash shows the segment-to-term pass recursing three frames per nesting level (`MakeTerm.go_s` → `unsorted` → `exp`); the frames are large enough that ~125 levels exhaust Chrome's ~1 MB main-thread stack. The `--profile dev` build crashes at ~100 levels, and the CLI already needs `node --stack-size=8192` for the same reason. The modular-editors branch happens to survive 200 nested `let`s because it parses each definition separately, but nested parentheses would still overflow there. Not bisected.

issue.title: Stepper and evaluator disagree on an indeterminate `if` reached through a filter (uncollapsed branch casts)
issue.body:
claude:

`[(), (debug () in if ? then () else B)]` — QCheck `Evaluator and stepper are consistent`, seed 773972249.

The stepper reaches the ascription push non-recursively (after `CompleteFilter`) and leaves uncollapsed casts inside the branches of the indeterminate `if`; branches are never evaluation positions again, so they stay. The evaluator's `req_final` path collapses them via `transition_multiple`. Both results print identically because casts are hidden; `Equality.semantic` counts them.

Opening the stepper on this program also crashes:

```
Failure("exp_idx: e1 not found in e2 (found 1 matches)")
```

#2408 originally carried a fix that made the `If` push case in `Ascriptions.re` collapse branch casts fully. Review (@7h3kk1d) was skeptical of deep-transitioning into a stuck `if`, so that change was dropped; the property itself is disabled on dev since #2482 (pinned as #2128). Whether the right fix is in the stepper's push order, in `Ascriptions.re`, or in making the equality ignore casts for this test is open.

issue.title: Modules II, part 7: a signature member declared twice is an error
issue.body:
Seventh of the stack, on top of #2501. A signature that declares the same member twice is now an error.

- The later declaration is marked with the new `SigDuplicateMember`: `type S = { let x : Int; let x : Bool }` reports `Member x is declared more than once in this signature` on `let x : Bool`. Value and module members share a namespace (`let m` and `module m` clash); type members, manifest or abstract, have their own, so `let x : Int; type x = Int` is fine.
- The mark lives on the signature item itself. `Info.sig_` gains `marks`, which `Info.marks_of` now reads, so the cursor inspector, the problem sidebar and `hazel analyze` all report it; the CLI caret covers the whole item.
- Module bodies are unchanged: a repeated binding there is shadowing, last wins, as before.

Slide item 23a shows the error. Tests cover value, manifest type, abstract type, manifest-then-abstract, module, and value-versus-module duplicates, the shared and separate namespaces, and that the later item carries the mark.

`make test-quick` green · the Modules slide analyzes with errors only under its "Error" items.

issue.title: Modules II, part 5: tuple label errors like modules, named missing members, CLI spans
issue.body:
Fifth of the stack, on top of #2498. Improvements to error reporting that reach beyond modules, kept apart from the module fixes in parts 1 and 3.

- **Labeled tuples follow the module design for bad projections.** `t.y` with no label `y` now marks the label (`LabelNotFound`, now worded "Tuple has no label y; its labels are x") while the dot carries only a message (`Message.TupleLabelNotFound`), the same shape part 1 gave `m.y` on modules and the type-level `M.Fake` always had. Applies to tuples and lists of tuples.
- **Missing members are named for any signature-typed expression.** When an expression of signature type is analyzed against a signature that declares members it lacks, `StaticsBase.expectation_mismatch_mark` reports `ModuleMissingMembers` instead of a generic type mismatch, so a module variable, a function argument, or a function result names what is missing, as a module literal already did. The computation is shared through `Sig.missing_members`. Slide item 26a shows `greet(Carol)` with `Carol` lacking `name`.
- **CLI carets span the whole diagnosed term.** `hazel analyze` used to underline only the tile carrying the term's id, so `M.x + 1`'s error pointed at a single `.`. The caret now covers every measured id of the term (`m.x`, `a + b`, a module literal on one line), matching what the editor highlights; terms inside folded projectors keep the location-less fallback without spurious lookup warnings.

issue.title: Modules II, part 4: module-typed functions and generative escape
issue.body:
Fourth and last of the stack, on top of #2495. Functions take and return modules with abstract types; a path cannot escape the scope of its root.

- **Avoidance.** `Typ.avoid` runs at function bodies, `let` bodies (so `module … in` too) and each `case` arm. A module path rooted at the binder going out of scope is first reduced in the body's context, so a manifest member simply expands. A path that is still abstract stays abstract as an escaped type (see below), except that a signature member defined as that path becomes abstract and later members refer to it by name. So `fun (m : S) -> m` has type `S -> S`, `fun (m : S) -> m.x` has an escaped abstract type as its result, and each call of a function returning a module with abstract members yields a fresh type (generativity). Inside the scope `m.x : m.T` is unchanged; the part-3 tests that pinned root types now read the in-scope type from the info map.
- **Sibling paths.** The signature walk binds value member names as well, so a member typed by a sibling module's abstract type projects as `M.Inner.T` instead of silently becoming `?`. A written-out signature left behind by a type alias (`{ type T = Int }.T`) also projects.
- **Runtime.** A cast to an abstract path type is a no-op: elaboration normalizes manifest paths away, so a path reaching the runtime is abstract. Before, `let z : m.U = m.y` left the stuck value `1:m.U`.
- **Editor.** Deleting the `=` of a signature `type T = Int` downgrades the tile to the bare abstract form (the inverse of part 3's upgrade), leaving the old definition dangling as a stray type to remove or reattach by retyping `=`. `Editing.SigAbstract` grows to 34 cases: typing the bare form, adding `=` in every position, removing it backward, forward and by selection, round trips, and a MakeTerm-level check of the resulting item kinds.
- **Property test.** The QCheck AST generator emits signature types (with a shrinker), and a new property checks that no binder inside a random program leaks into its root type.

**Doc slide.** The split into `modules.hz` and `module-signatures.hz` now lands in part 3; this part adds section G (module-typed functions) to the second slide. Background: adding that section to the combined slide overflowed the JavaScript stack in the CLI. It is not a loop: statics in jsoo overflows node's default stack at roughly 100 plain nested `let`s (about 10 to 16KB per level), and the combined slide had about 70 nesting levels plus 30 `module` bindings. The C3 build needed a stack between 950 and 984KB for it and this one between 984 and 1000KB, against a default of 984KB. The slide is now two: `modules.hz` (construction, qualified types, signatures, errors) and `module-signatures.hz` (width subtyping, abstract types, module-typed functions), both registered in `Slides.re`. The stack depth itself deserves an issue.

## Avoidance keeps the type abstract

Where a path outlives its root, avoidance used to fall back to unknown, and
unknown is consistent with everything, so the loss was silent: nothing told
the author, and every later use checked against nothing. It now mints an
escaped abstract type (`Typ.Escaped`), which is consistent with `?` and with
itself and inconsistent with everything else. That is the relation an
in-scope abstract member already has, so no new rule is invented; what is new
is a representation that survives the loss of its root, generalizing the
clause avoidance already had for signature members.

```
let get = fun (m : BOX) -> m.x in get(B) + 1
-- This has the abstract type m.T, which escaped the scope of its module,
   so it cannot be used where a concrete type is required

let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in dup(ShowInt, "s")
-- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
   mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature,
   to keep the caller's type
```

Binding an escaped value, passing it to an unannotated function and giving it
to a hole all still work: the error appears where the author wrote something
concrete, which is the gradual half of the bargain.

- **The parameter is closed too.** The function arm avoided only its body, so
  a component annotated with an earlier component's member left the type
  mentioning a binder no caller can name, and every argument passed, since
  normalization maps a path with an unbound root to unknown. Only the copy
  that becomes the function's type is closed; the pattern's own type and the
  elaborated ascription keep the precise path, so runtime casts and
  incremental-evaluation keys do not move.
- **Generative per application.** `Typ.freshen_escaped` gives each call its
  own identity, so two calls of one function escape different types and
  joining them is an error, while a value bound once and used twice is fine.
  Identities are derived from the application's id rather than generated, so
  re-checking an elaboration still yields an equal type.
- **`Mark.EscapedType` says which side escaped**, so the advice fits the
  case, and an escaped type displays as its path plus a short tag of its
  identity, since two escapes of one path are different types. A failed
  implicit resolution keeps erasing to unknown (`Typ.escape_to`): that
  failure is already marked, and opacity there would only cascade.
- **Not fixed here:** what the caller knows, that the parameter is a
  particular module, still cannot be written in an ordinary arrow type. An
  implicit binder can hold it (#2508); an ML sharing constraint for ordinary
  module parameters is the missing feature. A tuple argument also still
  reports the component and the tuple, which is the pre-existing cascade
  fixed off-stack in #2502.

Two commits: the type form, inert, with its `meet` rules and traversals; then
minting, the closed parameter, freshening and the diagnostics. The escape
tests in the modules suite now assert the escaped type where they asserted
unknown, five new cases cover the behavior, slide item 42 keeps its abstract
type and 43 shows the error.

## Fixes the fuzz properties turned up

Three defects, each found only through a Slow-tagged QCheck property and so only on seeds that generated the shape — parts 5-8 went red while this part stayed green on the very same bugs. Each now has a deterministic test, so the seeds no longer decide.

- **A cyclic alias crashed the analysis.** `type x = x.a in ?` aborted with `weak_head_normalize exceeded 1000 recursive calls`. `TyAlias` already guards self-reference by wrapping the definition in `Rec`, and normalization leaves a `Rec` alone — but from this part `x.a` is a module member projection, so normalizing it asks `path_sig`, and `as_sig` unrolls that `Rec` looking for a signature, handing the projection straight back. Out of fuel the type now comes back unreduced, stuck, which is what the function already returns for everything else it cannot reduce; the program reports `Expected a module or tuple type, found type rec x -> x.a`. `Typ.CyclicAlias` pins it.
- **A printed `:` glued to a leading-plus sum.** `Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` failed on `(()) @< ({ let _:+ Adid }) >`: `:` is an operator character and `Token.is_potential_operator` matches any run of them, so `:+` lexes as one token that is no form at all, while Menhir's separate lexer splits it. `should_add_space` already knew this hazard, but as a list of two characters (`$`, `!`) rather than the property they share; it now asks `Token.begins_with_potential_operator`, which covers `!` along with every other operator character. `$` stays listed, being a name character. An unparenthesized sum only ever reaches a `:` as a sig member's ascription, which is why this appears here.
- **Printing was not idempotent.** `type T = { … }` printed as `({ … })`, then `(({ … }))`, a layer per trip. `parenthesize_typ`'s `Parens` case ran its own content through `paren_typ_at(Precedence.min)`; precedences count down from `max = 0`, so that test wraps exactly the types whose precedence *is* `min` — a Sig, a bare sum, a multihole — and re-wrapped them every pass. The wrapper being emitted is already the protection: nothing outside can bind into it. **Not specific to modules** — `dev` grows the same layers on a parenthesized bare sum (`type T = (+ Adid) in 7`), so this fixes that too and carries it along with the stack.

## Known gaps

- **No dependent domain for ordinary module parameters.** An explicit
  parameter cannot be named later in its own parameter list or in the result
  type, which is exactly the equation this PR reports the loss of. An
  implicit binder (#2508) is the only construct that can hold it, so marking
  the parameter implicit is the current substitute for a sharing constraint.
- **No existentials with an unpacking form.** An escaped abstract type is now
  a real type rather than unknown, but there is no way to give one a name and
  use it, so such a value stays inert. Storing modules with differing
  abstract members in a list, or returning one from a conditional, therefore
  still loses the shared type.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (~~3658~~ 3809 tests) · `Statics.Properties` (crash and closedness properties, with signatures generated) and `MenhirFuzz` pass · both slides analyze with errors only under their "Error" items · the Menhir and elaboration properties also pass at the five seeds that had been failing (803422318, 57351729, 931683130, 541095201, 92308926) · `make ci-check` clean under the release profile.

issue.title: Incremental eval leaves a binding unsubstituted when evaluation gets stuck after an edited literal
issue.body:
## Summary

The QCheck property **"Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit"** (`test/evaluator/Test_Evaluator_Properties.re:307`, `~count=2000`) fails for some seeds. It presents as a flake, but it isn't: given a program of the right shape it fails **every time**. Only whether QCheck generates that shape is random.

Minimal repro, no seed needed:

```hazel
{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }
```

Edit the `4` to `5` (which is what the property does — a type-preserving `+1` on an int literal), then evaluate the edited program two ways:

| | result |
|---|---|
| fresh (no `prev`) | `let true = A in (x=(()))` |
| incremental (`prev` = original's `incr_eval`) | `let true = A in (x=x)` |

Both get stuck on the failing pattern match `let true = A`, as expected. The disagreement is in the residual environment: **fresh has substituted `x`'s value, incremental has left `x` as a variable.** `Equality.semantic.exp` then reports them unequal, which is what fails the property.

## Required ingredients

Removing or reordering any of these makes it pass, which should localize it:

- **A named binding before the literal.** `let x = ()` fails; `let _ = ()` passes — the name has to survive into the residual.
- **The literal bound to `_`.** `let _ = 4` fails; `let y = 4` passes.
- **Evaluation must get stuck *after* the literal.** `{ let true = A; let _ = 4 }` (stuck first) passes.
- **Stuck via a pattern-match failure, not an unbound variable.** `let true = q` passes; `let true = A`, `let true = ()`, `let false = A`, `let 7 = A` all fail.

Irrelevant: the literal's value (`0` and `4` both fail), and the number of preceding bindings — `{ let x = (); let z = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` fails with `(x=x, z=z)` against `(x=(()), z=(()))`, so every named binding is affected, not just the first.

## Seeds

`QCHECK_SEED=3` and `QCHECK_SEED=468045375` both reproduce via the property itself; `QCHECK_SEED=1` and `2` pass. Seed 3 shrinks to

```
(0, { let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A; type y = y; type ? = Bool; type x = Void })
```

and the three trailing type aliases are incidental — the minimal case above is what's left after removing them.

## Why this matters now

This is a **second** flaky-looking property, distinct from #2128 ("Evaluator and stepper are consistent"). #2422 makes the test runner propagate a real exit status, so from that point a tripped property **blocks** rather than merely annotating a green run. With `~count=2000` and no fixed seed, both will start failing PRs intermittently.

Two things worth deciding alongside a fix: whether the residual should substitute (fresh's behaviour looks right, but that's a call for whoever owns incremental eval), and whether these properties should carry a fixed seed in CI with randomized seeds in a periodic run, so a real regression is distinguishable from a newly-unlucky draw.

## Reproducing without QCheck

The helpers the property uses are all top-level in `Test_Evaluator_Properties.re` (`collect_int_lits`, `replace_int_lit_by_id`, `statics_and_elab`, `eval_limited`), so the case above can be driven directly from parsed text — which is how it was minimized, and probably how it should be pinned as a regression test once fixed.

issue.title: Author tutorial lessons as .hzt text
issue.body:
Stacked on #2250, with #2513 on top. **All three PRs in this stack are meant to be merged together** — they are split for review only.

## Summary

Adopts the text-authored tutorial system from `probes-study-rebuilt` and converts all 25 lessons to it.

Each lesson used to be an `.ml` file holding a serialized zipper alongside its prose — ~26,000 lines of generated data that had to be regenerated by hand for any edit. Lessons are now plain-text `.hzt` files in `hazel-programs/tutorial/`, embedded with `ppx_blob` via a new `src/tutorialslides` library (a clone of `src/docslides`) and parsed into `Tutorial.spec` at startup by `TutorialText`:

```
@title      the lesson name
@flags      wrapper show_report version=N id=<uuid>
@prompt     markdown for the instructions panel
@hint       one-liner
@reference  markdown for the Task Reference sidebar
@hints      one per line
@code       editor contents (holes are ¿, or ? to survive a container)
@test       hidden tests
```

Net: **+2,855 / −26,285**.

The conversion was mechanical. `TutorialDecode` reads whatever lesson list is compiled in and emits `.hzt` via `MarkerParse.to_text`, so the CLI landed first and generated all 25 from the existing `Tu_*.ml`. `./hazel tutorial-verify` checks that each slide's impl and tests are a fixed point of `to_text ∘ of_text ∘ to_text`; all 25 are. `TaskRefDocs` is gone — decode inlines each lesson's composed `task_reference` into its own `@reference`.

One marker is ours rather than upstream's: **`@title`**. Upstream derives the title from the filename, which would renumber every lesson and mangle four of them (`Reverse Function Application (Pipelining)` losing its parens; `and`/`of` capitalising). `@title` pins the exact title and falls back to the derived one.

## Bugs the round-trip check surfaced

- **`$==` in the Case Expressions and Folding Lists hidden tests.** `$` does not lex in Hazel, so those six tests were unsatisfiable and always reported indeterminate — a live bug the serialized form hid. Now `==`, and both suites pass.
- **`[¿]` in List Literals** collapsed to `[]` on reparse, losing the fillable hole. Explicit `[?]` round-trips.
- Stray trailing grouts in five hidden-test cells.

## Tutorial-mode chrome

Also ports the styling/UX work from that branch:

- a collapsible **Tasks** section, split from the prompt at its `Task` header (all 25 lessons now have one)
- the hint as a keyed `<details>`, so its open state no longer leaks across slides
- first/last slide nav gating — **required**, since `.hzt` `version` defaults to 1 and the old `version > 1` / `version < 10` gates would break
- SAND background, focus-driven cell accent, `{{video:}}` and `{{no_editor}}` prompt markers
- per-slide scroll memory, and driving the slide `<select>` from the model so it follows keyboard navigation
- `Zipper.caret_to_start`, so `@code` loads with the caret at the start of the program

`show_report` changes meaning under the new `show_task_ui` gate — it now marks a slide as a *task* (grading face + report icon) rather than "start with the report panel expanded" — so it is set on the six converted lessons that have real hidden tests. Only Probes, whose sole test is `test true end`, leaves it off.

Four general CSS fixes come along: a broken pin-icon URL in `style.css` (which sits in `www/`, so `../img/` resolved outside it), the test sigil's `z-index` (it painted above projector overlays), `nowrap` on context-menu items, and overscroll containment so a nested horizontal scroll does not fire the browser back-gesture.

## Deliberately left behind

`TutorialProbeStrip` and `TutorialSlideInit` — both are exhaustive hardcoded tables over that branch's own slide ids and need `AutoProbe.t` plus new `ProbeProj.Settings` variants — and the probe/evaluator/Card rework they depend on.

## Test plan

- [x] `make dev` builds clean
- [x] `make test-quick` — 3465/3465
- [x] `./hazel tutorial-verify` — 25/25 slides round-trip cleanly
- [x] All 25 lessons in the dropdown, in order, with their exact original titles
- [x] Tables driven to 3/3 passing; Folding Lists to 3/3 (previously impossible)
- [x] Tasks + Hint collapsibles, grading face and panel, prev/next gating, Task Reference sidebar

issue.title: Incremental eval leaves a binding unsubstituted when evaluation gets stuck after an edited literal
issue.body:
## Summary

The QCheck property **"Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit"** (`test/evaluator/Test_Evaluator_Properties.re:307`, `~count=2000`) fails for some seeds. It presents as a flake, but it isn't: given a program of the right shape it fails **every time**. Only whether QCheck generates that shape is random.

Minimal repro, no seed needed:

```hazel
{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }
```

Edit the `4` to `5` (which is what the property does — a type-preserving `+1` on an int literal), then evaluate the edited program two ways:

| | result |
|---|---|
| fresh (no `prev`) | `let true = A in (x=(()))` |
| incremental (`prev` = original's `incr_eval`) | `let true = A in (x=x)` |

Both get stuck on the failing pattern match `let true = A`, as expected. The disagreement is in the residual environment: **fresh has substituted `x`'s value, incremental has left `x` as a variable.** `Equality.semantic.exp` then reports them unequal, which is what fails the property.

## Required ingredients

Removing or reordering any of these makes it pass, which should localize it:

- **A named binding before the literal.** `let x = ()` fails; `let _ = ()` passes — the name has to survive into the residual.
- **The literal bound to `_`.** `let _ = 4` fails; `let y = 4` passes.
- **Evaluation must get stuck *after* the literal.** `{ let true = A; let _ = 4 }` (stuck first) passes.
- **Stuck via a pattern-match failure, not an unbound variable.** `let true = q` passes; `let true = A`, `let true = ()`, `let false = A`, `let 7 = A` all fail.

Irrelevant: the literal's value (`0` and `4` both fail), and the number of preceding bindings — `{ let x = (); let z = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` fails with `(x=x, z=z)` against `(x=(()), z=(()))`, so every named binding is affected, not just the first.

## Seeds

`QCHECK_SEED=3` and `QCHECK_SEED=468045375` both reproduce via the property itself; `QCHECK_SEED=1` and `2` pass. Seed 3 shrinks to

```
(0, { let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A; type y = y; type ? = Bool; type x = Void })
```

and the three trailing type aliases are incidental — the minimal case above is what's left after removing them.

## Why this matters now

This is a **second** flaky-looking property, distinct from #2128 ("Evaluator and stepper are consistent"). #2422 makes the test runner propagate a real exit status, so from that point a tripped property **blocks** rather than merely annotating a green run. With `~count=2000` and no fixed seed, both will start failing PRs intermittently.

Two things worth deciding alongside a fix: whether the residual should substitute (fresh's behaviour looks right, but that's a call for whoever owns incremental eval), and whether these properties should carry a fixed seed in CI with randomized seeds in a periodic run, so a real regression is distinguishable from a newly-unlucky draw.

## Reproducing without QCheck

The helpers the property uses are all top-level in `Test_Evaluator_Properties.re` (`collect_int_lits`, `replace_int_lit_by_id`, `statics_and_elab`, `eval_limited`), so the case above can be driven directly from parsed text — which is how it was minimized, and probably how it should be pinned as a regression test once fixed.

comment.body:
Recording another occurrence, filed separately as #2499 before I'd connected it to this issue — it should be closed as a duplicate of this one. Unlike the two occurrences above, this one is **the same shape**, and it also happens to confirm one of the ingredients.

**Run:** [33941773846](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33941773846), `Full tests` on `fumola-livelit-mvp` (#2492) at `05be2f0276` — `qcheck random seed: 955690280`, `1 failure! in 751.689s. 3752 tests run.` The branch diff is livelit/projector/rendering code and touches no evaluator code. Same commit passed the full suite locally, twice.

Shrunk counterexample (1 shrink step):

```
(6, { type x = (); let _ = 0; type ? = ?; let _ = B; type ? = Bool; type x = ();
      let y = 0.193974; let _ = 1; type y = (); let A = 1261828.579156; let ? = A })
```

## It's this bug, not a second shape

I drove this expression through `check_incremental_against_fresh_after_edit` on #2482's branch rather than reasoning from the printout:

```
Expected: `let A = 1261828.579156 in let ? = A in (y=0.193974)'
Received: `let A = 1261828.579156 in let ? = A in (y=y)'
```

That's the residual-substitution disagreement in this issue exactly — fresh substitutes the named binding, incremental leaves it a variable — with `(y=0.193974)` / `(y=y)` standing where the minimal case has `(x=(()))` / `(x=x)`. All four ingredients hold: named binding `y` surviving into the residual, the edited literal bound to `_`, stuck after the literal, and stuck via a pattern-match failure (constructor `A` against a float value, rather than `let true = A`).

## Incidental confirmation of the "named binding before the literal" ingredient

The expression has two int literals, `let _ = 0` and `let _ = 1`, and `seed = 6` selects one of them. Editing one disagrees; editing the other passes.

`collect_int_lits` prepends onto its accumulator, so its list runs backwards relative to traversal — index 0 is the *last* int literal in source order, `let _ = 1`. That's the one `6 mod 2 = 0` picks, and it's the one that fails. The named binding `let y = 0.193974` sits immediately before it. Editing the other literal instead (`~literal_index=7`, i.e. `let _ = 0`, which no named binding precedes) makes the two agree and the check pass.

So this counterexample carries its own negative control, and it lands the way the ingredient list predicts. Worth noting because the two occurrences above both looked like they might not fit — this one does, and the ordering requirement is load-bearing rather than an artifact of how the minimal case was reduced.

## For the pin in #2482

Doesn't change anything there — `{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` is still the cleaner pin. But once #2482 lands this property is skipped and the case index shifts, so seed 955690280 stops being reproducible by re-running the group; keeping it recorded here is the point. I've left a note on #2499 about the renumbering.

```

3752 is the full count — the same number the run produced locally, where everything passed. So this is one property failing, not a run that died.

- The same commit passed locally: 3752 tests, exit 0 (539.7s), and again on a rebuild.
- The branch's diff is livelit/projector/rendering code. The generators do not produce the term forms it touches.
- Earlier in the same branch's life, two *other* properties in this group failed in about 11 local runs — three distinct properties failing across runs points at the group rather than at any one property.

### Possibly related

The shrunk counterexample has the same flavor as #2372 (duplicate binders): `type x = ()` twice, `type ? = ?`, a constructor-shaped binder holding a float (`let A = 1261828.579156`), and `let ? = A`. That is a guess from reading the term, not a diagnosis.

Also in the same family: #2372, #2287.

### Cost so far

A change on this branch was reverted in response to a red build from this group, and the revert turned out to be unnecessary — the failure was the flake, not the change. A red `Evaluator.Properties` currently cannot be distinguished from a real regression without re-running.

### Not verified

- Whether the seed reproduces locally (the machine was busy with a full run when this was written).
- Whether it reproduces on `dev`. #2397 and #2287 both do, so branch-independence is likely but untested here.
